essays.stem: A Kingston manufacturer must announce a two-week delay on a major export order. Plan how it should communicate the delay to the overseas buyer, its bank and its own staff.
essays.modelAnswer: The firm should first confirm the facts: the cause of the delay, the new delivery date, and what it is doing to recover. It should agree one consistent message and who speaks for the firm. The overseas buyer must hear first and directly, through a call or video call from the senior account manager, followed the same day by a formal email or letter. This should apologise, explain the cause briefly without blaming others, give the new date, set out the steps taken to protect quality and any offer to reduce the impact, such as part shipment. The bank needs a short, factual briefing from the finance manager, since the delay affects cash flow; it should show the revised cash forecast and whether any extra facility is needed, so the bank is not surprised. Staff should be told at a team briefing what has happened, what it means for their work and overtime, and what they may and may not say to outsiders. The firm should then keep each group updated at agreed times until delivery is made.
markingPoints: Confirms facts and agrees one consistent message and spokesperson
Buyer told first, directly, then in writing; apology, reason, new date, recovery steps
Bank briefed factually by finance with revised cash position
Staff briefed on impact and what they may say outside
Plans regular updates until the issue is resolved

essays.stem: A key supplier wants to raise its prices by 12%. Plan how you would prepare for and conduct the negotiation.
essays.modelAnswer: I would prepare by gathering facts: what we buy from them each year, their past prices, current market prices from other suppliers, and their likely reasons, such as higher import or fuel costs. I would work out our interests (stable supply, quality, a predictable cost), our best alternative if no deal is reached, such as a second supplier, and our walk-away point, for example no more than 6%. I would also think about the supplier's interests, such as prompt payment and a larger, longer contract. At the meeting I would build rapport, ask open questions to understand the reasons for the rise, and listen carefully. Rather than arguing about one figure, I would look for trade-offs: a smaller rise phased in over the year, a longer contract, larger orders, faster payment, or a change in delivery arrangements. I would keep calm, avoid accepting the first offer, and summarise each point agreed. Finally, I would confirm the agreement in writing, with the price, dates and conditions, and plan a review before the contract ends.
markingPoints: Gathers facts on volumes, market prices and the supplier's reasons
Sets own interests, BATNA and walk-away point; considers the supplier's interests
Uses rapport, open questions and listening at the meeting
Seeks trade-offs (phasing, contract length, volume, payment terms) rather than haggling on one figure
Summarises and confirms the agreement in writing, with a review date

essays.stem: Evaluate the use of credibility, logic and emotion when persuading a hotel board to fund a staff wellness programme.
essays.modelAnswer: Credibility comes from the speaker and the evidence. A manager who knows the hotel, has run a small pilot or brings in a respected health professional is more likely to be believed. Without credibility, even good figures may be doubted, so it is the foundation. Logic is likely to carry most weight with a board, which must justify spending. The manager should show the costs of the programme and the expected benefits in figures: lower sick days, less staff turnover and the cost of recruiting and training replacements, and perhaps better guest scores. A payback calculation and a pilot result would be persuasive. Emotion has a place too: a short, true example of a staff member whose health improved, shared with permission, reminds the board that staff are people and links to the hotel's values. However, emotion used alone, or overdone, can look manipulative and weaken the case. The best approach combines all three: a credible speaker, a strong logical case at the centre, and a brief emotional touch that makes the figures memorable.
markingPoints: Credibility: source of trust (speaker, pilot, expert) and why it is the foundation
Logic: costs, benefits in figures, payback, pilot results; key for a board
Emotion: true example used with permission, linked to values
Evaluates risks of overusing emotion or lacking credibility
Recommends a balanced combination with logic at the centre

essays.stem: Explain the main barriers to communication with people outside the organisation, and how a manager can overcome each.
essays.modelAnswer: Language barriers arise when the other party speaks a different language or does not know our technical terms. The manager can use plain language, explain terms, and use a qualified interpreter or translation where needed. Cultural barriers come from different customs about greetings, directness, time and hierarchy; researching the other culture and asking respectfully when unsure helps. Physical and technical barriers include poor phone or internet links, noise and distance; choosing the right channel, testing technology and confirming key points in writing reduce them. Perception barriers occur when people interpret a message through their own expectations or past experience, for example a client who already distrusts the firm. Active listening, checking understanding and building a relationship over time help. Information overload is common: busy clients ignore long messages, so keep them short, put the main point first and use headings. Emotional barriers, such as anger after a complaint, block listening; acknowledging feelings and staying calm come first. Finally, a lack of feedback hides misunderstanding, so the manager should invite questions and confirm agreement.
markingPoints: Language/jargon barriers and solutions (plain language, interpreters)
Cultural barriers and solutions (research, respect)
Physical/technical barriers and solutions (channel choice, testing, written confirmation)
Perception, overload and emotional barriers with suitable solutions
Importance of feedback and checking understanding

essays.stem: Compare a formal letter, a business report and an email as ways of giving a client a full response to a serious complaint. Recommend one, with reasons.
essays.modelAnswer: An email is fast, cheap and easy to reply to, and suits short updates and confirming arrangements. For a serious complaint, though, it can seem casual, is easily forwarded, and long emails are often skimmed. A formal letter, sent by post or attached to an email on letterhead, shows that the firm takes the matter seriously. It suits a full response: acknowledging the complaint, apologising where right, explaining what was found, and setting out the remedy and the steps taken to prevent a repeat. It can be signed by a senior manager. A business report is the most detailed format, with headings, findings and recommendations. It suits an investigation that the client or a regulator needs to see in full, but it can feel impersonal and too long for most clients. For a serious complaint, I recommend a formal letter signed by a senior manager, sent as an attachment with a short covering email so it arrives quickly. If an investigation was done, a summary of its findings can be included in the letter or attached. A phone call before the letter helps to show care.
markingPoints: Email: fast and easy but may seem casual and is skimmed or forwarded
Formal letter: shows seriousness; suits a structured response; senior signature
Report: most detailed, suits investigations, but may be too long or impersonal
Recommends a formal letter (possibly attached to an email) with clear reasons
Mentions content of the response (acknowledge, apologise, explain, remedy, prevention) or a call first

essays.stem: A food contamination scare affects a restaurant chain in Montego Bay. Describe how management should communicate with the media, customers and staff in the first 48 hours.
essays.modelAnswer: Management should first bring together a small crisis team, put the crisis communication plan into action and name one trained spokesperson. Public safety comes first: any affected product is withdrawn and the health authorities are informed and worked with. Within a few hours, a short holding statement should be issued to the media and on the firm's own channels. It should say what is known, show concern for anyone affected, explain the immediate steps taken, and promise further updates at set times. It must be accurate and avoid guessing or blaming. Customers need clear advice: which outlets or dates are affected, what symptoms to look for, where to get help, and how refunds will be handled, with a phone line or page for questions. Social media should be watched and answered calmly with the same facts. Staff should be briefed before the public statement where possible, told what has happened, what to do and what to say, and directed to send all media enquiries to the spokesperson. Over the 48 hours, the team should give regular updates, correct false reports and record every communication.
markingPoints: Forms a crisis team, uses the plan, names one spokesperson
Puts safety first and works with the health authorities
Prompt, accurate holding statement showing concern, with update times
Clear advice and contact channel for customers; social media monitored
Staff briefed early with a clear media rule; regular updates and records kept

essays.stem: Describe how a manager should prepare for and hold a difficult conversation with a business partner whose service has fallen below the agreed standard.
essays.modelAnswer: The manager should first gather the facts: the agreed standard in the contract or service agreement, and specific examples with dates where service fell short, plus their effect on our business. She should decide what outcome she wants, such as a recovery plan within a month, and what she will do if it is not met. She should arrange a private meeting, in person or by video, at a time that allows a proper discussion, and tell the partner the purpose in advance so they are not ambushed. In the meeting, she should open by valuing the relationship, then describe the problem calmly using the facts and their effect, without personal blame. She should then ask for the partner's view and listen, since there may be causes she does not know, such as problems on our side. Together they should agree specific actions, responsibilities and dates, and how progress will be checked. She should close on a positive note, then confirm the agreement in writing and follow up at the agreed time.
markingPoints: Gathers facts: agreed standard, specific examples, impact
Decides the desired outcome and fallback; arranges a private meeting with notice
Opens positively and describes the problem factually without blame
Asks for and listens to the partner's view
Agrees actions with dates, confirms in writing and follows up

essays.stem: Explain how a manager should adapt her communication when dealing with overseas clients and when dealing with people who have disabilities.
essays.modelAnswer: With overseas clients, she should research their business culture in advance: how formal greetings and titles are, whether they prefer direct or indirect speech, attitudes to time and deadlines, and who makes decisions. She should speak clearly, avoid local slang, idioms and jokes that may not translate, and confirm key points in writing, since written English is often easier to follow than fast speech. She should check time zones and public holidays when arranging calls, and use a qualified interpreter or translation for detailed or legal matters. With people who have disabilities, she should ask what works best for each person rather than assume. Documents can be offered in large print or in formats that work with screen readers; meetings can use captions or a sign language interpreter; venues should be accessible. She should speak directly to the person, not to a companion or interpreter, and use respectful, people-first language. In both cases, the aim is the same: remove barriers so the message is fully received, show respect, and check understanding.
markingPoints: Overseas clients: research culture (formality, directness, time, decision-making)
Overseas clients: clear speech, no slang, written confirmation, time zones, interpreters
Disabilities: ask the person what works; accessible formats, captions, interpreters, venues
Speaks directly to the person and uses respectful language
Links both to removing barriers, respect and checking understanding

essays.stem: Evaluate the benefits and risks of using social media and messaging apps for business communication, and recommend rules for a firm.
essays.modelAnswer: Social media lets a firm reach many customers quickly and cheaply, show its products, answer questions and build a community. Messaging apps are fast and popular in Jamaica, and suit quick updates with customers and teams. These channels also give useful feedback on what customers think. The risks are real, however. Posts spread fast and are hard to remove, so one careless or offensive message can damage the firm's name. Complaints are public and can grow if handled badly. Mixing personal and business accounts blurs boundaries, and staff may share confidential or personal data by mistake. Messages on personal phones may be lost when staff leave, and records may not be kept. I recommend clear rules: only named, trained staff post for the firm; posts follow the brand style and are checked for accuracy; complaints get a polite public reply and are moved to a private channel; no customer or staff personal data is shared, in line with the data protection law; business messaging uses accounts the firm controls; and staff keep personal opinions separate from the firm's accounts.
markingPoints: Benefits: reach, speed, low cost, community, feedback
Risks: fast spread, reputation, public complaints
Risks: confidentiality and personal data, mixing personal and business, lost records
Recommends clear rules: authorised staff, accuracy, complaint handling
Rules on data protection and firm-controlled accounts

essays.stem: Justify the ethical and legal limits a manager must respect when communicating on behalf of a business.
essays.modelAnswer: A manager speaks for the business, so what she says can bind it and affect its reputation. Honesty is the first limit: claims about products, prices, results or approvals must be true and supported, because misleading customers is unfair, may break consumer protection rules and destroys trust once found out. Confidentiality is the second: information given in confidence by clients, partners or staff must not be shared, and the firm's own sensitive plans must be protected. Personal information must be handled in line with the data protection law's general aims: collected for a clear purpose, used only for that purpose, kept secure and shared only when allowed. The manager must also avoid making damaging statements about people or competitors that she cannot prove, since this may be defamatory. She must respect others' intellectual property, not copying text, images or logos without permission. Finally, she must stay within her authority, not making promises or commitments that she is not allowed to make. Respecting these limits protects the business from legal claims and builds the trust that good communication depends on.
markingPoints: Honesty: true, supported claims; misleading claims are unfair and risky
Confidentiality of others' and the firm's information
Personal data handled in line with the general aims of the data protection law
Avoids unproven damaging statements and respects intellectual property
Stays within her authority; justifies limits by trust and legal protection

practical1.title: Negotiate a supplier agreement and confirm it in writing
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a negotiation case: a supplier of packaging (played by the assessor or another group) wants to raise its prices by 12% and change its delivery terms. Your group is the buying firm. First prepare a written negotiation plan with your interests, the supplier's likely interests, your best alternative (BATNA), your walk-away point and at least three possible trade-offs. Then hold a 20-minute negotiation meeting. Give each member a named role: lead negotiator, second negotiator (asks questions and proposes trade-offs), finance adviser (works out the cost of each offer in J$ from the figures given), note-taker (records offers and agreements), and observer (scores the group's use of listening, questions and assertive language on a checklist). In a group of four, the note-taker also observes. After the meeting, the group writes a formal letter confirming what was agreed. Photograph each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Negotiation case and figures from the assessor
Computer with word processor and printer
photos: The negotiation plan showing interests, BATNA, walk-away point and trade-offs
The finance adviser's cost workings for each offer
The note-taker's record of offers and the final agreement
checklist: Took a named role and prepared their part of the negotiation plan
Used open questions and active listening to find the supplier's interests
Proposed trade-offs rather than arguing over one figure
Used assertive, respectful language and stayed calm under pressure
Cost workings are correct and were checked twice
Confirmation letter is formal, accurate and matches the agreement
safety: Treat the other side with respect; the role play is about the issue, not the person
Use made-up firms and figures only
Keep the negotiation plan confidential from the other side until the meeting ends
Take a short break if the role play becomes stressful

practical2.title: Prepare a crisis communication pack and hold a mock media interview
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a crisis scenario for a made-up business (for example a power failure that spoils stock at a supermarket chain, or a bus from a tour company involved in a minor road accident). As a group, prepare a crisis communication pack within 2 hours, then hold a 5-minute mock media interview. Give each member a named role: plan lead (a one-page plan showing each audience, the message, the channel, the person responsible and the timing), press release writer, customer message writer (email and website notice), staff briefing writer (what staff should do and say), and spokesperson (takes part in the mock interview, asked by the assessor or another group). In a group of four, the plan lead also writes the staff briefing. Every document must give the same facts. Photograph each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Computers with word processor and printer
Phone or tablet to photograph or record the mock interview (with agreement)
Templates for a press release and a communication plan (optional)
photos: The customer email and website notice
The mock media interview in progress
All documents laid side by side to show the facts are consistent
checklist: Took a named role and produced their document on time
Messages are prompt, accurate and show concern, with no guessing or blame
Each audience gets the right channel, content and tone
Press release covers who, what, when, where and why, with a contact for updates
Spokesperson stayed calm, kept to the facts and did not speculate
Group checked that all documents give the same facts
safety: Use made-up businesses and people only; do not name real firms or victims
Record the mock interview only if every member agrees, and keep it within the Centre
Speak respectfully about anyone affected in the scenario
Share the time pressure fairly and take a short break after the interview
